title: BibVik Citation Analysis: Camps, Communities, and Citational Politics
text:
Citation detection per F1 paper





Distribution of outgoing (resolved) citation counts across the F1 corpus.




Every F1 paper has at least one resolved outgoing citation, and the citation graph as a whole forms a single connected component. This was not the case throughout corpus construction: extraction passes repeatedly left individual F1 papers disconnected, most often from a reference-list format (footnote-embedded citations, a shared reference section for an edited volume, non-Latin or corrupted encoding) the primary extraction method did not handle, or from the same work being independently extracted twice under two citekeys. Each case was resolved against the original source PDF or documented as a genuine structural exception.

title: BibVik Citation Analysis: Camps, Communities, and Citational Politics
text:
From detection to resolved bibliography
The citation graph is built in two stages: automated detection of candidate citations per paper, then manual correction and deduplication across the whole bibliography.



Raw citation detections by method, before merging duplicate detections of the same citation


Detection method
Raw detections




Structured reference list (GROBID)
22049


Inline citation markers
15484


LLM body-text scan
11644


Text-pattern matching
9094


LLM bibliography reparse
1818


LLM footnote scan
843





Each paper’s PDF is scanned by six independent methods: GROBID parsing its structured reference list, matching inline citation markers in the body text, text-pattern matching, and three LLM-based passes (a body-text scan, a bibliography reparse, and a footnote scan). A single real citation is frequently flagged by more than one method. The 60,932 raw detections above merge down to 29,786 deduplicated citations per-paper, which are then carried into the bibliography-wide correction process below. The structured reference list and inline-marker matching account for the large majority of raw detections; the LLM-based methods contribute the remainder, recovering citations the structured parser misses, most commonly footnote-embedded references and citations in non-standard or non-Latin formats. 1.16% of bibliography entries (167) have no title recorded: a paper in the corpus cites them, but the entry itself has no title or an incomplete author.
Once detected, citations are carried into a single shared bibliography, where the same underlying work can be independently detected from multiple citing papers and needs consolidating into one record. This consolidation, along with other manual corrections, is tracked in a running corrections file (corrections.yaml) rather than as edits to the raw pipeline output.



Manual, individually-reasoned correction actions applied to the bibliography (corrections.yaml)






Action
Count




set (field corrections: author, year, title, citer lists, etc.)
11736


delete (fabricated or unresolvable ghost entries removed)
1770


create (missing entries added from manually verified source data)
946


merge (duplicate entries combined)
246


reject (candidate merges/matches checked and confirmed distinct)
80


split (single entries separated into multiple genuine works)
19





Two bulk, mechanical field backfills are tracked in the same file but excluded from the table above: a language value was set on 12,807 entries and a detection value on 12,804 entries, both copied wholesale from the pipeline’s own processing cache rather than individually reasoned. Combined they account for more set actions than every other correction in the file put together, so are reported separately to avoid making the file’s manual-correction volume look larger than it is.
As of this writing the file holds 14797 individually-reasoned correction actions, plus the 25,611 bulk field backfills noted above. The great majority of delete actions removed “ghost” entries: records with no title and no raw citation text, produced when the extraction pipeline generated a placeholder entry it was never able to resolve to a real source. merge actions consolidated cases where the same underlying work had been independently created under two or more citekeys, most commonly because one version came from an automated reference-list extraction with no linked PDF and a second, fuller version was later created when the paper’s own PDF was located and processed directly, or because the same source was independently extracted from two different citing papers’ reference lists, the cross-paper duplication this section exists to resolve. set actions in the table above cover routine field-level corrections: fixing fabricated or garbled author names, correcting mis-parsed years and titles, and adding real citation relationships (cited_by entries) that automated detection missed or failed to resolve on the first pass.
One deletion in this file was subsequently confirmed incorrect and reversed: a genuine F1 paper had been marked fabricated across multiple earlier review passes despite being a real, verifiable source, and was restored with corrected metadata once checked directly against its source PDF. This is noted here as a reminder that delete corrections, like any other, should be treated as provisional until checked against a primary source rather than as settled fact on the strength of a confident-sounding note.

title: BibVik Citation Analysis: Camps, Communities, and Citational Politics
text:
Region










Matching to Wikidata
Region is free text drawn directly from each paper, not a controlled vocabulary: spelling variants and mixed specificity (continent, country, named site) count as distinct terms in the word cloud above. Wikidata is used to consolidate these to real places with coordinates. Pleiades, Pelagios/Peripleo, and iDAI.gazetteer were considered and set aside: all three are institutionally anchored in Mediterranean/classical-world antiquity, with no confirmed non-trivial coverage of Viking-Age Scandinavia. Wikidata was used instead for its dense, well-curated coverage of Scandinavian archaeological sites and structured multilingual labels/aliases, which handle spelling variants (Danmark/Denmark) close to for free.
The chunks below call Wikidata’s SPARQL endpoint and so require outbound network access; they default to eval: false and do not run on a normal render of this document. Run them explicitly (flip eval: true) when the lookup table needs building or refreshing, then leave them off again — the rest of this section reads the resulting static CSV, same as Topic, Method, and Source read their own derived data.
Coverage probe. Before matching all tokens, check hit rate on the most frequent ones — this is the actual empirical check for whether Wikidata is workable here, not an assumption.
Check probe_results before continuing. If the hit rate on real, frequent Viking-Age placenames (Birka, Hedeby, Kaupang, Ribe, Uppåkra, Tissø, etc.) is low, the class filter above may be too narrow — Wikidata items for archaeological sites are not always tagged with exactly these instance of values — and the SPARQL query needs revising before running the full match. A high count under contains fallback is expected and fine — it means the class filter is right but the corpus token is a shortened form of the item’s real label (e.g. “Gokstad” for “Gokstad Mound”), not a coverage problem.
Full match, once the probe above confirms acceptable coverage. This single chunk matches every token, separates out macro-region terms that can’t resolve to a point, and writes the resulting lookup table plus a manual-review export, all together (previously three separate chunks; merged into one so a single eval flag controls the whole matching-to- saved-file pipeline, since matching without saving the result was wasted work run for nothing):
Nesting (optional). Every matched place is currently flat: “Birka,” “Vestfold,” “Sweden,” and “Scandinavia” are independent tokens with no recorded relationship between them, even though Birka is genuinely in Uppland, Sweden, Scandinavia. This chunk resolves three nesting levels for each matched place, each as its own column:

admin_region — the first P131 (“located in the administrative territorial entity”) ancestor above the site itself, before reaching the country: a county, province, or similar (e.g. Birka → Uppland). Not every place has a clean single admin-region ancestor in Wikidata; those are left NA rather than guessed.
country — walked further up P131* to the first ancestor that is itself a country (Wikidata class Q6256).
super_region — not derived from Wikidata at all. Unlike country, there is no single reliable Wikidata class for “super-region” in the sense this corpus uses the term (Scandinavia, British Isles, Baltic states); these are real, well-understood historical/cultural groupings, not administrative ones, so this is a small, explicit, hand-authored country → super-region mapping instead of an automatically-derived one. Extend super_region_map below as more countries appear in the resolved data.

Like the matching chunks above, this calls Wikidata and needs network access; it stays off by default.
Country resolution here runs on the raw matched coordinates, before the known_bad_matches correction is applied (that correction lives in region-joined below, and only nulls the bad matches’ lat/lon/etc. there, not here). So resolving nesting right after this chunk can produce a real country value for a token later corrected to no_match — e.g. “Repton” resolving to “United States” here, even though region-joined clears it entirely downstream. That correction was extended to also null admin_region/country/super_region when present, so this is handled automatically as long as region-joined runs after nesting, which it always does on a normal render.
Once region_lookup.csv exists, the resulting region_df joins region to gender, topic, method, source, and year the same way those variables already join to each other elsewhere in this document — by cite_key, using the same Wilson-interval and by-year machinery.


Where the corpus is set
Most of the real signal in Region is simply where papers are concentrated geographically — a stacked gender-composition bar chart like the ones used for Topic, Method, and Source needs several well-populated categories to say anything real, and Region has one (Birka, 20 papers) with a steep drop to a long tail of 1-3-paper tokens, so that chart type doesn’t suit this variable the way it suits the others. Two more direct views instead: where the named, point-matched places actually are, and how concentrated the corpus really is by raw count.
What the map includes. A region token appears as a point only if it has a real matched coordinate, is not a macro-region term (Scandinavia, Viking world, East Baltic, and the rest of that list — excluded even when Wikidata does return a coordinate for the concept, since a single point can’t honestly represent an area that broad), and falls within a fixed plotting bounding box (lat 25-80, lon -60 to 100) that excludes a couple of real but geographically irrelevant matches (Oceania, Pacific Ocean) which would otherwise force the whole map out to a global scale. Dot size is the number of papers carrying that exact region token — 20 papers all tagged “Birka” produce one dot sized 20, not 20 separate dots. The map’s crop is computed from the real spread of whatever points pass all three filters, with a fixed margin, so it always fits what’s actually shown rather than a hardcoded guess.





Named places mentioned in the corpus, sized by number of papers. Macro-region terms (Scandinavia, Viking world, and similar) are excluded even when Wikidata returns a coordinate for them, since a single point cannot honestly represent an area that broad — see the totals chart below for those. Cropped to the real spread of the remaining matched coordinates with a margin; a handful of correct but far-flung matches (e.g. Oceania, Pacific Ocean — real tokens in the corpus, real Wikidata matches) fall outside this crop and are not shown on the map.









Every region token with at least 3 tagged papers, point-matched places and macro-region terms together, ranked by raw count.




By country (optional, requires country nesting). The chart above keeps every region token flat, “Birka” and “Sweden” and “Scandinavia” are three separate bars even though Birka is in Sweden — deliberately, since the paper’s own choice of a site-level or country-level term is itself part of what the data says, not noise to collapse away. This alternate view rolls site-level tags up to the country they’re actually in, using the country column added by the region-nesting chunk above (only present once that chunk has been run). A paper tagged “Birka” counts toward Sweden here even if it was never separately tagged “Sweden.” Macro-region terms (Scandinavia, Viking world) still have no single country and are excluded from this view.





Papers per country, site-level tags rolled up to their containing country.






Topic, method, and source by region
Same problem as gender composition above: most region tokens have too few papers to support a per-region proportion chart. Enrichment solves this differently — restricted to regions with at least 5 tagged papers, each cell shows that region’s coverage of a topic/method/source divided by that category’s own rate across the whole corpus (1.0x = corpus average), the same measure already used for cluster structure in Part 3. A region’s low paper count still means less certainty behind its cells, but enrichment at least says something real about direction even on a modest sample, where a stacked-proportion chart on the same sample would mostly just show noise. All three heatmaps below share the same region row order, so a region’s profile can be compared directly across tabs.

TopicMethodSource of evidence







Topic enrichment by region (regions with 5+ tagged papers only). White = topic at corpus average rate for that region; blue = above average; red = below. Cell shows raw count behind the percentage. Capped at 3x so a handful of extreme small-n ratios don’t wash out the rest of the scale.











Method enrichment by region (regions with 5+ tagged papers only). Same reading as the topic heatmap above.











Source-of-evidence enrichment by region (regions with 5+ tagged papers only). Same reading as the topic heatmap above.









Topic, method, and source by administrative level
The tabset above groups by the raw region token as written in each paper, “Birka” and “Sweden” stay separate rows even though one is inside the other. This section repeats the same topic/method/source enrichment analysis, but grouped at each of the three nesting levels resolved by the region-nesting chunk above instead: admin region, country, and super-region. Requires that chunk to have been run at least once — each tab below checks for its column and explains what to do if it’s missing.
The enrichment baseline here is different from the tabset above, on purpose: each cell compares a group’s rate against the rate among only the papers that resolved to some value at that nesting level, not against the whole 369-paper F1 corpus. The flat-token tabset above uses the whole-corpus rate, since every F1 paper is a fair comparison point for a raw region tag. Nesting-level resolution is a narrower subset (only papers whose region successfully resolved up to a country, say), so comparing against the whole corpus would dilute the baseline with papers that never entered this analysis at all and understate real enrichment within the resolved set. Enrichment numbers are therefore not directly comparable between the two tabsets, even when they group the same underlying papers.

By admin regionBy countryBy super-region




























































































Change over time
Does the corpus’s geographic focus shift across the years covered, more Iceland/Greenland work recently versus more mainland Scandinavia earlier, or the reverse? Same problem as the other region breakdowns: most tokens have too few papers spread across too many years to support a real per-year trend. Restricted to regions with at least 8 tagged papers (a higher bar than the 5-paper threshold used for the topic/method/source heatmaps above, since splitting an already-small group by year further thins each cell), using the same Wilson-interval and enrichment machinery already defined for Topic, Method, and Source.





Papers per year, per region (regions with 8+ tagged papers only). Faint bars: few papers that year.









Enrichment per year, per region (regions with 8+ tagged papers only) — that year’s coverage of the region, divided by the region’s own average coverage across the whole corpus (1.0x, dashed line = normal). Faint bars: few papers that year.

title: BibVik Citation Analysis: Camps, Communities, and Citational Politics
text:
Degree and centrality
In-degree (times cited within the corpus) and out-degree (number of works cited) capture different roles. High in-degree identifies widely-cited works — the intellectual anchors of the field. High out-degree identifies works that are heavily engaged with the literature, drawing on many sources.
Betweenness centrality identifies works that sit on many shortest paths between other works — brokers between sub-literatures. Betweenness is expensive to compute on large graphs; both normalized and raw values are reported. Normalized divides by the theoretical maximum for a graph this size (roughly (n-1)(n-2) for a directed graph), so on a graph with over 12,616 nodes even a genuinely high-betweenness work normalizes to a very small fraction — small in absolute terms, not because the work is unimportant. Raw values, not rescaled, are more intuitively legible for comparing works directly against each other.
PageRank assigns authority based on incoming links weighted by the authority of the linking node — conceptually similar to being cited by works that are themselves widely cited. Hub and authority scores (HITS) are complementary: hubs point to many authorities; authorities are pointed to by many hubs.
Peripheral works — low degree, low centrality by every measure below — are not treated as noise in this project. A work cited only once may be exactly the interesting case (a niche, contested, or newly emerging reference) for a study of citational politics. No node is excluded from any measure in this section on the basis of low degree.

Degree distribution
A power-law or scale-free degree distribution is characteristic of citation networks: most works are cited rarely, a small number are cited frequently, visible as a roughly straight-line decline on a log-log plot. The plot below tests whether this corpus follows that pattern.

AnnotatedAnnotated, seed filtered

























The bulk of the distribution follows a fairly straight decline on this log-log scale, consistent with the expected power-law pattern: most works are cited once or twice (86% of works with at least one citation in Annotated and 87% in Annotated, seed filtered), a much smaller number several times. In Annotated, 99% of works with at least one citation are cited eight times or fewer, and 99% in Annotated, seed filtered. The tail is real, not an artifact of a truncated plot axis: the maximum in-degree is 84 in Annotated and 84 in Annotated, seed filtered. Betweenness and publication year
A negative relationship between publication year and betweenness is expected as a baseline structural effect, independent of any specific work’s importance: an older work has had more time to accumulate citations from both earlier and later literature, giving it more opportunities to sit on shortest paths between clusters that didn’t yet exist when it was published. The interesting question is not whether that baseline trend exists, but what departs from it: works that are old without being especially well-connected, and, more notably, works that are young but already bridging despite limited time to accumulate citations — those are candidates for genuinely novel synthesis, not just structurally advantaged age.
The trend line4 in the first plot of each tab is fit to the nonzero subset, where the actual bridging signal is. In Annotated, 0 of the 359 works with nonzero betweenness (0%) were published before 2000. In Annotated, seed filtered, the figures are 0 of 230 (0%). The second plot in each tab shows every work, including the zero-betweenness majority, so the shape of any boundary between old and recent works is visible directly.

A work can have nonzero betweenness only when it both cites other works and is cited, and only the annotated papers cite anything here. The works with nonzero betweenness were published between 2000 and 2021, although 47% of all works in Annotated predate 2000. 12,246 works in Annotated and 12,148 in Annotated, seed filtered are only cited, and 0 and 0 of them have nonzero betweenness. Older works therefore score zero whatever their place in the literature, and these plots cannot compare old and recent works. Among the works that can score, the Spearman correlation between publication year and betweenness is -0.17 in Annotated and 0.08 in Annotated, seed filtered, where a negative value means earlier works have higher betweenness.

title: BibVik Citation Analysis: Camps, Communities, and Citational Politics
text:
K-core decomposition
The k-core of a graph is the maximal subgraph in which every node has at least k connections to other nodes within that subgraph. It is computed by iteratively removing nodes with degree below k until no further removal is possible. A node’s coreness is the highest k for which it still belongs to the k-core: a coreness of 1 means the node only survives the weakest possible core (removed as soon as k reaches 2), while a high coreness means the node stays embedded even as the graph is stripped down to only its most densely-interconnected parts.
K-core decomposition is reported here purely as a descriptive measure, showing which works sit in dense mutual-citation relationships versus which sit at the periphery, following Alvarez-Hamelin et al. (2005). Every work, regardless of its coreness, is still included in full in every other analysis in this document: coreness only describes a work’s position, it doesn’t filter anything out.
Coreness and in-degree measure genuinely different things, worth comparing directly: in-degree simply counts how many times a work is cited, with no regard for whether those citing works are themselves well-connected. Coreness asks a structurally deeper question, whether a work sits inside a neighborhood that is itself densely interconnected, not just cited often in isolation. A work could have high in-degree while sitting at low coreness, if most of its citations come from otherwise peripheral, poorly-connected works; conversely, a work with only moderate in-degree can have high coreness if it’s embedded in a tightly interlinked core. The tables below show whether these two measures broadly agree on this corpus, or diverge in informative ways.

title: BibVik Citation Analysis: Camps, Communities, and Citational Politics
text:
Community detection
Community detection here produces several independent descriptions of how the graph divides, not a single answer to be triangulated. Louvain (Blondel et al. 2008) and Leiden (Traag, Waltman, and Eck 2019) ask “which groups of nodes are more densely interconnected than a random graph with the same degree sequence would predict,” a notion formalized as modularity (M. E. J. Newman 2006). Girvan-Newman (Girvan and Newman 2002) asks “which edges, if removed, disconnect otherwise-separate parts of the network.” K-means asks a third, differently-grounded question again: not about graph structure at all, but about each work’s centrality profile, grouping works that occupy similar structural positions, for example highly-cited authorities vs. high-betweenness brokers vs. peripheral works.

Louvain, Leiden and K-means






Note



Louvain, Leiden and K-means are computed for both graphs in graph_metrics() with no visible output. Their agreement across the two graphs is reported in “What the seed filter changes”. The plotting code for each is kept in the appendix, disabled; toggle eval: true on any of those chunks to render it.




Girvan-Newman

How it works
Louvain and Leiden each partition the graph once, at one resolution, and return a single result. Girvan-Newman (Girvan and Newman 2002) instead removes edges one at a time: at each step, it identifies the edge with the highest betweenness centrality (the edge carrying the largest number of shortest paths between all pairs of nodes in the graph), removes it, and recomputes betweenness for the remaining edges before repeating. Because a shortest path between two densely connected regions of a graph usually has to cross whichever single edge joins them, that edge tends to have disproportionately high betweenness and is removed early, while edges internal to a well-connected region, which have many alternative paths around them, are removed only much later. The result is a record of the entire removal sequence, from the original, fully connected graph down to every paper standing alone: a dendrogram. The tree below is that record. Height represents the order in which components split apart, not the raw round number, since the actual rounds are spaced too unevenly to remain legible on a linear axis; left-right position carries no information and is arranged only to avoid crossing branches.

AnnotatedAnnotated, seed filtered



























Choosing a stopping point
Girvan-Newman, in its original form, does not select a stopping point from this sequence (Fortunato 2010); the removal process continues until no edges remain. A refinement published two years after the original algorithm (M. E. Newman and Girvan 2004) selects the round with the highest modularity score as the working partition, and this is the conventional choice, but it fails on this corpus: modularity continues to rise as the graph fragments, reaching its maximum only once 94.4% of nodes are singleton communities (94.3% of nodes in the seed filtered run), which is not a usable partition. This is a documented limitation of modularity on sparse networks, where it can lack a clear maximum and instead admit many different high-scoring partitions (Good, de Montjoye, and Clauset 2010). The criterion used instead counts connected components directly: the point where that count starts climbing steadily, one round after another, marks where the graph is actually breaking into pieces, independent of whether modularity happens to be rising or falling at the same time. The earliest such round is 7,532 (Annotated) and 7,905 (Annotated, seed filtered), and it is used for every community grouping in the rest of this document.

Community-level structure
The plots above show individual nodes coloured by community; none of them show which communities are strongly connected to which others, since edges are drawn identically whether they cross community boundaries or stay within one. This collapses each of the top 20 clusters to a single node, sized by its real membership count, with an edge between two cluster-nodes weighted by the real number of citation edges crossing between them in the original graph — the genuine inter-community structure, not individual-node detail.

A real edge here means real papers in one cluster actually cite, or are cited by, real papers in the other; its width is that count, not an estimate. A cluster with no edges at all in this plot is real too: it means none of the top 20 clusters share a direct citation tie with it, whatever thematic similarity a reader might expect from the labels alone.

Relations between clusters
The graph above shows how many citations pass between clusters, and that count depends heavily on how large each cluster is. This test asks whether the citations from one cluster land in another cluster more or less often than chance would put them there, for the 20 clusters in the graph. Each citing paper keeps its whole reference list, so one paper citing many works in the same cluster is not counted as many independent events. The shuffle moves every citing paper to a randomly chosen cluster, keeps the number of citing papers in each cluster, and counts again, 1000 times. A pair is flagged when the difference holds after a Benjamini-Hochberg correction at 0.05. Each cell reads from the citing cluster in its row to the cited cluster in its column, so the matrix is not symmetric.

Cluster labels
This section identifies each cluster’s most-cited papers by within-cluster citation degree, then has a language model write a label and description from their titles, independent of the F1 annotation codebook. Comparing these labels against the codebook happens separately, in 03_joined_descriptions.qmd.
For each cluster, select_representatives.py ranks the cluster’s own papers by how many other members of that cluster cite them, and takes the top few as a representative sample. label_clusters.py sends those titles to a language model, which sorts them into named groups and writes a label and description from the largest group; a second label is written only when a real second group exists with enough titles behind it. Full detail on both steps, including the hub-independence rule and the mechanical checks run on the model’s output, is in cluster_labelling/README.md.

Communities of communities
The clusters can be grouped in turn. Two clusters are linked when papers in one cite papers in the other, and also when their citing papers cite many of the same works. A single run of one community-detection method is a weak basis for groups here, because the result changes with the method, the resolution and the definition of a link. The grouping below therefore runs 8 variants, with 5 random seeds each, on every cluster of every size. The variants are Leiden at four resolutions, Louvain, Infomap on undirected and on directed links, and Leiden on shared references. Two clusters share a group when they were grouped together in at least 50% of the runs on average. A cluster forms a group alone when no other cluster meets that test with it, which means the variants disagree about which cluster it belongs with. Each group reports the share of runs in which its members stayed together. A high share is necessary but not enough, because weakly linked clusters can be grouped together consistently without sharing a theme, so the cluster labels in each row need reading as well.

Relations between groups
The groups relate to each other unevenly. For each pair of groups, the test counts the pairs of clusters, one from each group, that share at least one citation link. It compares that count with 1000 shuffles in which every cluster keeps its number of links to clusters in other groups and the partners are drawn again. Counting linked cluster pairs and not citations means one paper citing many works in another cluster counts once, and keeping each cluster’s links means groups full of heavily linked clusters do not look related to everything. A pair of groups links more or less than the shuffle when the difference holds after a Benjamini-Hochberg correction at 0.05. Only groups of two or more clusters are included.

title: BibVik Citation Analysis: Camps, Communities, and Citational Politics
text:
Appendix: layout trials
The partition plots above use the Fruchterman-Reingold layout (fr, 500 iterations, with igraph’s grid speed-up). The layouts below were tried and are kept for reference with eval: false. Each calls the same plotting function as the main plots, so any of them can be switched on one at a time and run on either graph.

fr spreads the papers that cite a hub around it, so each community reads as a region of the plot. It runs in seconds on either graph.
lgl with coolexp lowered to 0.5, the layout used before, stretches the graph into one diagonal band and leaves the highlighted communities overlapping through its middle. It is also far slower than fr on the seed-filtered graph.
drl stacks the papers that cite a hub on top of it, so every community collapses into a single dot and the plot shows nothing of its shape.
stress (graphlayouts::layout_with_stress()) is faster than drl and built to preserve graph distance. It produced a concentric-ring pattern and was rejected.
Untuned lgl places a handful of true outliers far from the rest. That is why the main plots crop the view to the 1st to 99th percentile.
lgl with repulserad doubled spread the periphery out and left the inner core dense. repulserad sets the distance at which repulsion stops acting and does not change its strength, so it is the wrong lever for core density.

The Louvain, Leiden and K-means plots, also disabled. Each saves a PNG and a PDF next to this document.

section: Cluster structure vs. topics, methods, and sources of evidence
text:
Cluster structure vs. topics, methods, and sources of evidence
community_gn (Girvan-Newman, fragmentation-onset cut) is checked here against the topics, methods, and sources of evidence coded in Part 1, for both versions of the graph. Annotated uses the cut of the Annotated run and Annotated, seed filtered uses the cut of the seed-filtered run. The comparison is restricted to works with a matching annotation (F1-only; see the join above), which is 369 works in Annotated and 369 in Annotated, seed filtered. Louvain and Leiden cluster assignments also exist from Part 2 but are not used in this section.
Coverage is thin relative to the graph as a whole: in Annotated, 369 annotated works out of 12616 nodes, and within any single cluster that annotated count is often a small fraction of the cluster’s real size (the heatmaps below show only the 20 clusters with the most annotated works, and even those may have only a handful of annotated works out of a much larger true membership). A prior exploratory pass on an earlier GN cut of this same corpus found 7-13 annotated nodes per cluster typical, out of hundreds of members, and treated agreement between structure and annotation as directionally suggestive rather than comprehensively verified for that reason. The same caution applies here: what follows can show that structure and coding line up somewhere, but cannot rule out that the uncoded majority of any cluster tells a different story.
The coded columns are wide, one column per topic/method/source category, valued "Primary", "Secondary", or blank. Primary and secondary are merged throughout what follows: a work counts as coded with a category at either level, matching the method used in a prior exploratory pass on an earlier GN cut of this corpus. A work can carry more than one topic, method, or source, so per-cluster percentages below do not sum to 100%; each cell shows the raw count behind its percentage for transparency.
How to read the enrichment heatmaps below. Raw coverage (what fraction of a cluster’s annotated works carry a given category) is misleading on its own: some categories are common across the whole corpus regardless of cluster — “Spatial analysis” as a method, or “Environment” as a topic, show up in most clusters simply because most works in this corpus use them, not because any one cluster is distinctively characterized by them. To separate genuine distinctiveness from corpus-wide popularity, each heatmap cell instead shows enrichment: a cluster’s coverage of a category divided by that category’s rate across the whole annotated corpus. A value of 1x means the cluster carries the category at exactly the corpus average; 2x means twice the corpus rate; 0.5x means half. White is 1x (baseline); blue is above baseline (the category is over-represented in that cluster, a real distinguishing signal); red is below baseline (under-represented). For example, if “Palaeoenvironment reconstruction” is coded in 23% of the whole corpus but 100% of a given cluster’s annotated works, that cell shows roughly 4.4x — a real signal that environmental method is disproportionately concentrated there, not just present because it’s common everywhere.

By topic
Girvan-Newman clusters by topic. A threshold of 3+ annotated works lets through only a small share of the clusters in this corpus (see the counts below), so it does not give a workable set. Shown here instead, in the heatmap below: the 20 clusters with the most annotated works. This is a readability choice, not a derived breakpoint.
At this cut, Annotated has 402 clusters, 14 of which pass a 3+ annotated-works threshold, and its largest cluster is 89 members larger than the second-largest. Annotated, seed filtered has 1,013 clusters, 7 of which pass the threshold, and its largest cluster is 38 members larger than the second-largest.
Coverage varies a lot by cluster (annotation is thin relative to true cluster size, per the caveat above), so each row label shows how many annotated works its percentages are based on, out of the cluster’s true total size.

title: BibVik Citation Analysis: Camps, Communities, and Citational Politics
section: Cluster signatures: peak count and peak strength
text:
Cluster signatures: peak count and peak strength
Throughout this section, “cluster” means a Girvan-Newman graph cluster (community_gn), not a scholarly or social cluster.
The topic, method, and source enrichment findings above surface individual standout cells one at a time. This section combines them into two directly interpretable numbers per cluster, so the clusters most worth a closer look surface first instead of requiring a manual scan across three separate tables.
A peak is any category (topic, method, or source) whose 95% Wilson confidence interval on a cluster’s coverage rate lies entirely above the corpus-wide rate for that category — meaning the cluster’s coverage is higher than baseline with reasonable statistical confidence, not just a higher raw count. This adapts to sample size automatically: a cluster with only 3 annotated works needs a much larger raw enrichment to register as a peak than a cluster with 13, because a small sample’s interval is wider. This is the same criterion used in the topic, method, and source findings above (ci_lower > corpus_rate); “peak” here just names a category that already met that bar, so this section’s peak count and mean enrichment are computed directly from the same standouts listed there, not a separate pass.
For each cluster, two numbers: how many peaks it has, and how strong those peaks are on average. Neither is combined into a single score — peak count times mean enrichment is not a real, interpretable unit, and collapsing two different kinds of signal into one number invites over-reading it. Plotted directly instead: clusters with many peaks AND high average enrichment are worth reading first; a cluster with one very large but isolated peak is a different kind of finding (a strong single signal) than one with several moderate peaks (a broader, possibly more coherent pattern) — the plot keeps that distinction visible rather than flattening it. Whether a cluster’s peak categories actually cohere thematically is a judgment that requires reading them against domain knowledge of this corpus, which this plot does not attempt.

title: BibVik Citation Analysis: Camps, Communities, and Citational Politics
text:
Considering alternative units of analysis
Everything in this document treats the paper as the unit of the graph (papers cite papers). This is one particular projection of a richer structure, not the only one, and is worth extending in future work — not resolved or prioritized now, but recorded so it isn’t lost:

Author-level graphs. Collapsing papers into authors changes what centrality means (a prolific author becomes a hub independent of any single paper’s standing) and makes author-to-author citation homophily a more natural unit than paper-to-paper for gender-citation questions. Co-authorship itself becomes an additional structural question: do co-authorships cross or reinforce whatever divisions appear elsewhere.
Venue-level graphs (journal, edited volume, conference proceedings, grey literature/excavation report). Likely to reveal institutional or disciplinary structure rather than intellectual structure directly, and could complicate a purely topic/gender reading — a “camp” might partly reflect which kind of venue a sub-field mostly publishes in, particularly given the corpus’s substantial non-English, non-journal material (excavation reports, conference proceedings).
Kind-of-work as a unit (monograph vs. article vs. excavation report vs. edited-volume chapter). Related to venue but not identical; may track disciplinary/generational norms that could explain or cross-cut part of any gender/topic pattern rather than sitting alongside it as a fully independent axis.

Each alternative unit would be, again, an independent description rather than a more “real” or authoritative one. A useful way to stress-test any finding at the paper level is to check whether it persists, sharpens, or dissolves when re-aggregated to authors or venues — if a division only appears at one level of aggregation, that is itself informative about whether the division is fundamentally about individual works, about people, or about where people publish.

title: BibVik Citation Analysis: Camps, Communities, and Citational Politics

Citation functions

Analysis of the context surrounding citations to ascertain their functions
Analysis of citation groups to ascertain how authors represent others’ work in relation to each other

title: BibVik Citation Analysis: Camps, Communities, and Citational Politics
text:
Footnotes


The proportion of possible edges that actually exist: edges present divided by every pair of nodes that could be connected. Low density is normal and expected for a citation network — most works don’t cite most other works.↩︎
A weakly connected component treats every edge as undirected: two nodes are in the same component if a path connects them in either citation direction. This is the more forgiving of the two measures here.↩︎
A strongly connected component requires an actual directed path in both directions between two nodes. Rare in citation networks, since citations are historically directed — a 2010 paper cannot cite a 2020 paper — so most strongly connected components are single isolated nodes.↩︎
A LOESS fit, not a strict linear one, to allow for a non-constant relationship across the full year range rather than forcing a single slope.↩︎

title: A Protocol for Analyzing Citational Practice in Viking Age Archaeology
text:
The problem with counting citations
Citations are not neutral. They are rhetorical acts.
A citation can:

Provide evidence for a claim
Establish a methodological lineage
Set up a contrast or foil
Signal membership in a scholarly community
Exclude or render invisible

Standard bibliometric tools count that something is cited.
They cannot tell us why or how.

This connects to the workshop’s theme of citational politics.
Counting who cites whom captures network structure but not the work that citations perform.
A citation count tells you nothing about whether a reference is being invoked as evidence, as a foil, or as a gesture of acknowledgment.

title: A Protocol for Analyzing Citational Practice in Viking Age Archaeology
text:
What BibVik asks

How do various perspectives on the origins of the Viking Age manifest in the citation record?
Are these perspectives rooted in personal or professional identities and relationships?
How are citations used to situate one’s research in relation to prior work?


All of these questions posed by the BibVik project require something standard bibliometric tools don’t provide.
You can map citation networks, but you can’t tell from a network what a cluster represents intellectually, or whether a citation is being used as a support or as a foil.

title: A Protocol for Analyzing Citational Practice in Viking Age Archaeology
text:
The seed paper


Lund & Sindbæk (2022), “Crossing the Maelstrom: New Departures in Viking Archaeology”

Review of shifting paradigms in Viking Age research
574 bibliographic references
Authored by scholars representing different, yet converging, research traditions
Supplemented by seven anonymous peer reviewers who recommended additional sources


Generational model:



Generation
What it contains




P
Seed paper


F1
Papers cited by P


F2
Papers cited by F1


F3+
… and so on





How do we build a dataset that can address these questions?
We can’t survey the entire field — we need a principled entry point and a strategy for expanding outward.
Lund and Sindbæk’s review works because of how it was produced.
The two authors come from different research traditions, so the bibliography isn’t skewed toward one perspective.
And seven peer reviewers actively recommended additional references and challenged the authors’ characterizations.
So this isn’t just two people’s view of the literature — it’s been vetted by a panel of specialists.
From there we expand generationally.
The seed paper’s references are the first filial generation, their references are the second, and so on.

title: A Protocol for Analyzing Citational Practice in Viking Age Archaeology
section: Why not use open scholarly metadata?
text:
Why not use open scholarly metadata?

These data were never intended to be used for bibliometric analysis
Analysis tends to follow the variables readily at hand, rather than being driven by research questions



Scopus, Web of Science, OpenAlex, CrossRef — all tested, all insufficient
Poor coverage of monographs, edited volumes, grey literature, non-English sources — Viking Age archaeology is all of these



We need to generate data tailored for our questions, originating straight from their sources of origin, i.e. the publications themselves


But why not just use open scholarly databases such as Crossref, like everyone else?
The short answer is that these databases were never designed to be analysed.
They’re publisher registries and DOI assignment systems.
Studies end up analysing the handful of variables they provide because they’re available, not because they answer the research question.
Sampling and quality assurance are surprisingly uncommon in bibliometric work.
For our corpus, the coverage problem alone is especially troubling — monographs, edited volumes, and grey literature in Scandinavian languages are exactly what these databases handle worst.
But even with perfect coverage, the variables on offer wouldn’t enable us to answer our questions.
So we decided to generate our own dataset, and build the analytical structure around what we actually need.

title: A Protocol for Analyzing Citational Practice in Viking Age Archaeology
text:
Our analytical protocol

Creating a citation graph — structuring who cites whom, across generations
Extracting citation contexts — capturing the actual words around each reference
Interpreting citation functions — classifying the rhetorical work each citation performs
Detecting relationships between sources — characterizing how co-cited references relate
Identifying gaps and assessing coverage — measuring what we can’t see


Our protocol currently has five interdependent components, and I’ll go over each of these briefly.

title: A Protocol for Analyzing Citational Practice in Viking Age Archaeology
text:
Creating a citation graph
Which works are cited, and by whom?

Extract structured references directly from PDFs
Cycles through a few methods: regex, GROBID and LLM
Explicitly account for humanities citation conventions that standard tools miss

Citations in footnotes, citations embedded in prose, etc

Remove duplicates and redundancies


Rather than relying on any single extraction method, we apply five different detection methods to every paper and merge the results.
GROBID is a machine learning system trained on scientific journal articles that gives us easy access to structured bibliographic data.
However it is trained on a limited dataset that excludes much of what constitutes our corpus.
So we supplement this by also scanning the body text independently with regular expression patterns for standard citation forms, and with a local LLM for discursive references that do not fit a standard pattern.
This is especially useful for extracting references from footnotes or from contexts where they are embedded in prose.
All five methods run on every paper.
The results are merged and deduplicated — the same work cited across multiple papers with slightly different metadata resolves to one entry.
In practice, the additional methods catch 10 to 40 percent more citations than the reference list alone, and for some papers where GROBID fails entirely, they’re the only source of data.

title: A Protocol for Analyzing Citational Practice in Viking Age Archaeology
text:
Creating a citation graph



Extract bibliographic metadata into a flat data file, using BibLaTeX elements
Each work appears once, assigned a unique citekey
Names, titles and other values are normalized, even when different papers use slightly different spelling or formatting
Each contains a record of every paper that cites it


{
  "citekey": "sindbaek2007",
  "entry_type": "article",
  "title": "The Small World of the Vikings",
  "author": [
    {"family": "Sindbæk", "given": "Søren M."}
  ],
  "journaltitle": "Norwegian Archaeological Review",
  "volume": "40", "pages": "59--74",
  "date": "2007",
  "generation": "F1",
  "cited_by": ["lund2022", "aannestad2018"]
}


Here’s what a record looks like in our citation graph.
It uses common variables from the de facto BibLaTeX standard, each entry has its own unique citekey, and names and titles are normalized across the dataset.
What makes this different from just another bib file is the cited_by variable, which tracks every paper that references this work and makes this a relational dataset.

title: A Protocol for Analyzing Citational Practice in Viking Age Archaeology
text:
Extracting citation contexts
Where and how is each reference is invoked?
With the graph in place, we can locate where each reference is invoked — and capture what the citing author actually says.
{
  "context_id": "ctx_lund2022_sindbaek2007_001",
  "verbatim_text": "Recent studies have drawn on network theory to
    reframe Viking-period exchange as polycentric rather than
    hub-driven (Sindbæk 2007; Barrett 2010). This shift has
    implications for how we understand the relationship between
    centres like Birka and Hedeby and their wider hinterlands.",
  "citing_citekey": "lund2022",
  "cited_citekey": "sindbaek2007",
  "co_occurring_citekeys": ["barrett2010"]
}
Extracts the verbatim text — not a summary.
And the co-occurring references — what company each citation keeps.

For every citation marker in every paper, we extract the surrounding text — the actual sentences the author wrote when they invoked that reference.
The window adapts: usually a paragraph, but it extends across boundaries when needed, for instance when a reference is at the end of a paragraph it might capture the beginning of the next paragraph too.
We also record which other references appear in the same passage.
Sindbæk and Barrett appear together here — that co-occurrence, grounded in a specific passage, is what feeds the relationship detection later on.

title: A Protocol for Analyzing Citational Practice in Viking Age Archaeology
text:
Interpreting citation functions
Why is each reference cited, and how is it characterized?
{
  "context_id": "ctx_lund2022_sindbaek2007_001",
  "citation_function": "theoretical_framing",
  "citation_function_explanation":
    "The citing authors invoke Sindbæk's network model as the
     conceptual framework that reoriented the field away from
     centre-periphery models of Viking-period exchange. The
     citation positions this work as a paradigm shift rather
     than an incremental contribution.",
  "confidence": "high",
  "analysis_mode": "content_enriched",
  "characterization_assessment": "selective",
  "characterization_explanation":
    "Sindbæk's paper also addresses small-world network
     properties and their implications for information flow,
     which the citing authors do not engage with. The citation
     foregrounds the exchange dimension to serve the chapter's
     focus on material culture circulation."
}

This is the core analytical contribution.
A local language model reads each citation context and classifies the rhetorical work the citation performs.
The explanation matters more than the label — it’s grounded in the specific language of the passage.
For instance, here Sindbæk 2007 is classified as theoretical framing: invoked as a paradigm shift, not just a finding.
And we’re still experimenting with this, but when we have the full text of the cited work, the analysis can go deeper by comparing the citing passage against what Sindbæk actually wrote.
In this case, the model found that the citation of Sindbæk 2007 was somewhat selective because his paper also addresses information flow and small-world properties, but the citing authors foreground only the exchange dimension.
That gap between how a work is cited and what it actually says is exactly the kind of citational practice this project aims to make visible.

title: A Protocol for Analyzing Citational Practice in Viking Age Archaeology
text:
Interpreting citation functions: the prompt

You are an expert in academic citation analysis. Your task is to analyze how a cited work is being used in its citing context.
Context: The following is a passage from an academic paper. The citation of interest is marked with [target citation]. Other cited works may appear in the same passage.
{context_text}
The target citation refers to: “{cited_title}” by {cited_authors} ({cited_year}).
Task: Analyze the function of this citation. Consider these common citation functions as a starting point, but do not limit yourself to them:
[controlled vocab and definitions]
Respond in JSON format with exactly these fields:
[JSON template]


I want to be explicit about what the model receives.
It gets the text, some metadata about the cited work, a set of preliminary categories, and an instruction to return structured output.
It does not connect to the internet or any other database, and each run is independent of prior runs, so the model retains no memory of previous contexts.

title: A Protocol for Analyzing Citational Practice in Viking Age Archaeology
text:
Detecting relationships between sources
How do authors situate prior work in conversation?
{
  "cluster_id": "cluster_007",
  "members": ["barrett2010", "sindbaek2007", "ashby2015", "skre2007"],
  "relationship_type": "theoretical_conversation",
  "relationship_name":
    "Competing models of Viking-period network formation",
  "rationale":
    "Barrett and Sindbæk are cited together to propose
     network-based models emphasizing polycentric exchange.
     Skre represents an older centralized-hub model that
     the citing author positions as a foil. Ashby provides
     the empirical data from comb production used to
     adjudicate between these frameworks.",
  "directionality":
    "Barrett and Sindbæk build on each other; both contrast
     with Skre; Ashby provides evidence for evaluation.",
  "strength": "strong"
}

Two references co-occur when they appear in the same citation context.
Repeated co-occurrence (≥2 contexts) suggests the citing author sees a relationship.


Co-citation analysis typically stops at frequency.
We go further by asking what kind of relationship the co-citation encodes.
The LLM names the specific character of these relationships — not simply that these are similar.
For example, Barrett and Sindbæk propose network models, Skre is positioned as a foil, Ashby provides the evidence.
This is grounded in the actual passages, not inferred from counts alone.
And like with our other experimental method, when we have the full text of each cited paper, we can ask whether the citing author’s grouping reflect how these works actually relate.
Citations don’t just reflect intellectual relationships — they construct them.

title: A Protocol for Analyzing Citational Practice in Viking Age Archaeology
section: Detecting relationships between sources: the prompt
text:
Detecting relationships between sources: the prompt

You are an expert in academic citation analysis and bibliometrics. Your task is to analyze a group of references that frequently appear together in academic citations, and characterize the nature of their relationship.
Co-cited references: The following references frequently appear together in citation contexts: {reference_list}
Citation contexts where they co-occur: {contexts_text}
Citation function data: {function_data}
Task: Analyze the relationship between these co-cited references.
Consider:

Are they doing similar work (parallel findings)?
Is one building on another (methodological or theoretical lineage)?
Are they being used as contrasts or foils for each other?
Do they address complementary aspects of a problem?
Are they part of a theoretical conversation or debate?
Is there another type of relationship?

Respond in JSON format with exactly these fields: [JSON template]


Again, here’s the prompt for characterizing relationships among co-cited sources.
The model sees the actual references, the actual passages where they co-occur, and the citation functions identifying during the previous stage.
Like with the controlled vocabulary in the previous prompt, the six relationship types specified here are prompts for consideration, not a closed taxonomy.

title: A Protocol for Analyzing Citational Practice in Viking Age Archaeology
text:
Coverage and corpus assembly
How complete is our corpus?
This module:

Identifies success rates for each detection method applied to all records
Attempts recovery of missing references through online queries (Crossref, OpenAlex)
For F2, download open access content via the Unpaywall API, and estimate how much manual effort is required to complete the corpus


The final component closes the loop.
Reference extraction is imperfect, and if we don’t measure what’s missing, those gaps propagate silently throughout the rest of the pipeline.
Aggregating what works and does not work throughout the corpus may also tell us which methods work best for which kinds of documents, and help us streamline the process as we move forward.
For references that are detected in the text but missing from the bibliography, we attempt to “fill in” those records by tapping the CrossRef and OpenAlex APIs.
And for extending this to another F2 generation, we check open access availability via the Unpaywall API to estimate how much of that next layer we can acquire automatically.

title: A Protocol for Analyzing Citational Practice in Viking Age Archaeology
section: Why use an LLM at all?
text:
Why use an LLM at all?
The BibVik protocol considered several options:







Approach
Limitation




Manual coding
thousands of references across hundreds of documents


Scite Zotero plugin
Biased toward “neutral mention”, limited corpus


Jurgens (2018)1 2 open-source NLP
Requires NLP expertise to implement


Local LLM (this toolkit)
Focused on specific tasks, auditable, all data stays local



The LLM is not replacing human judgment.
It provides a systematic annotation that surfaces patterns for human review.

So now it’s time to address the elephant in the room:
Why are we using an LLM at all?
We first considered several alternatives.
Manual coding would be great in theory, we this is simply unrealistic given our extremely large corpus.
Scite is a product made by some data science firm and uses machine learning to do some very simple sentiment analysis, trained on recent STEM journal articles.
Aside from its mis-matched scope, Scite tends to play it safe by over-identifying neutral mentions.
A few researchers have developed tools to do similar work, but, personally, I can’t make heads or tails of any of it due to my own inexperience with NLP methods.
The local LLM gives us a way of generating targeted classifications, in way that’s relatively accessible, auditable, and secure.

Jurgens, David, Srijan Kumar, Raine Hoover, Dan McFarland, and Dan Jurafsky. 2018. “Measuring the Evolution of a Scientific Field through Citation Frames.” Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics 6: 391–406.https://github.com/davidjurgens/citation-function.

title: A Protocol for Analyzing Citational Practice in Viking Age Archaeology
text:
Limitations of LLMs

No domain-specific training in citation analysis
No calibrated confidence (high/medium/low is a heuristic, not a probability score)
Cannot detect implicit or distributed citation functions
Each context is classified independently — no cross-context reasoning
LLMs are slow, especially when using non-specialized hardware
At temperature 0.3, results are mostly reproducible, not guaranteed


At the same time, of course there are some limitations.
The model has no domain-specific training — it’s applying general reading comprehension to a specialized task.
The confidence labels are self-assessments, not calibrated probabilities.
Each context is classified in isolation, so the model can’t track how the same source is used across different parts of a paper - which may actually be a benefit, depending on what you’re trying to do.
LLM are very slow, especially when using older or off-the-shelf hardware.
And there are some limits on reproducibility, but overall trends in such a large corpus will probably remain relatively consistent across runs.

title: A Protocol for Analyzing Citational Practice in Viking Age Archaeology
text:
Next steps

Full run on the complete F1 corpus (many hours on a decent laptop)
Human review of a stratified sample of LLM classifications
Integration with the qualitative annotation protocol
Exploratory statistical and network analyses of the LLM classifications
Extend to F2 generation as coverage permits


After we refine the protocol based on a small subset, we will run it on the full F1 corpus.
This can be very slow - generating the citation graph alone for only 50 papers took about five hours, so the complete run will take a few days using my three year old laptop.
After that, we will do a human review of a stratified sample, integrate with the qualitative annotation protocol presented earlier, and dive into a network analysis to uncover systemic behaviours.
If time, resources and data availability permit, we may even extend this to another generation of works.

title: Bibliometric network analysis of Viking Age research (BibVik)
text:
BibVik is a project concerned with identifying trends in the published archaeological literature corresponding with shifting attitudes concerning the origins of the Viking Age. Specifically, we address how research on various topics relating to the origins of the Viking Age manifests in the published record, including associations between various topics, methods and sources of evidence; how these modes of inquiry are related to researchers’ personal or professional identities and relationships; and how citations are used to situate one’s research in relation to prior work.
We implement critical approach to bibliometric research methods. We recognize that open scholarly metadata, which is a bedrock of most modern bibliometric research, has intrinsic limitations that make it unsuitable for our analysis, and so we are experimenting with strategies for generating original data tailored for our research questions. In this sense, BibVik is also a response to the limitations of bibliometric research, and presents a vision for doing more meaningful, critical, and explicitly feminist work in this domain.
This website hosts our preliminary research protocol, manuscript preprints, and other relevant materials. All content is hosted and tracked at github.com/zackbatist/BibVik.
